partner_context.their_ambition: WSF is the largest ferry system in the US - ~24M riders/yr, 10 routes, 20 terminals - and is already electrifying. Washington State Ferries, a division of the Washington State Department of Transportation, is the largest ferry system in the United States - an essential part of the state highway system carrying ~24 million riders a year across Puget Sound and the San Juan Islands on 10 routes and 20 terminals.
partner_context.their_pressure: WSF is converting its fleet to hybrid-electric and building shore charging at up to 16 terminals - the largest hybrid-electric ferry program in North America. Growth and the net-zero mandate both demand fleet renewal without disturbing the services people rely on today.
partner_context.where_navier_fits: Navier is the zero-emission, software-defined passenger-only foiling layer above WSF's auto-ferry backbone - fast, frequent, low-wake hops on the busy Seattle-side commuter channels (Bainbridge, Bremerton, Kingston, Vashon) that complement the electrifying auto fleet, plus quiet access on the wake- and orca-sensitive San Juan waters.

hero.title: A zero-emission ferry network for Puget Sound
hero.subtitle: A foiling tier above today's ferry network on Puget Sound and the San Juan Islands: faster, near-silent, low-wake lines, a clear decarbonization path, and the services people rely on left running underneath.
hero.what_we_do_together: Navier is the zero-emission, software-defined passenger-only foiling layer above WSF's auto-ferry backbone - fast, frequent, low-wake hops on the busy Seattle-side commuter channels (Bainbridge, Bremerton, Kingston, Vashon) that complement the electrifying auto fleet, plus quiet access on the wake- and orca-sensitive San Juan waters.

why_now: A zero-emission foiling tier is a natural passenger-only complement to the auto-ferry electrification program: fast, low-wake hops on the high-demand commuter channels, opening frequencies the big auto boats can't run economically. WSF is converting its fleet to hybrid-electric and building shore charging at up to 16 terminals - the largest hybrid-electric ferry program in North America. A demo vessel is on the water now.
multimodal_fit: Navier slots into the network as the fast marine mode on Puget Sound and the San Juan Islands — feeding the existing rail, metro and bus interchanges and adding lines toward the authority's published growth and net-zero targets.

proof_points.evidence: Routes incl. Seattle-Bainbridge, Seattle-Bremerton, Edmonds-Kingston, Mukilteo-Clinton, Fauntleroy-Vashon-Southworth, Pt Defiance-Tahlequah, Port Townsend-Coupeville, and the Anacortes-San Juan Islands network (Lopez, Shaw, Orcas, Friday Harbor).

proof_points.evidence: WSF is converting its fleet to hybrid-electric and building shore charging at up to 16 terminals - the largest hybrid-electric ferry program in North America.
proof_points.source: WSF 2040 Long Range Plan; Washington state greenhouse-gas reduction & clean-transportation goals

proof_points.evidence: Hydrofoiling, software-governed vessels — the same DNA arriving in autonomous road mobility — built for fleet operation.

proof_points.claim: The fleet model is real and at scale.

objections.concern: Does this compete with the auto-ferry backbone?
objections.response: No — Navier is a passenger-only foiling layer above the auto ferries, adding fast frequencies on the commuter channels the big boats can't run economically. It complements the fleet electrification already underway.
Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal at existing piers — no new shore power, vertiports or rights-of-way.

objections.concern: Is foiling safe in busy, shared public waterways?
objections.response: Foiling is software-governed — geofenced no-foil and low-wake zones near piers, ferry lanes and moorings, automatic speed and wake limits in shared water, and conventional low-speed handling everywhere it isn't cleared to fly.

phases.label: Phase 1 — Seattle commuter-channel pilot
phases.rationale: Start where demand is already proven — the busiest commuter corridors, upgraded to faster, zero-emission foiling vessels.
phases.narrative: A focused commuter pilot on Puget Sound and the San Juan Islands — proving the foiling tier in sheltered home waters, additive to the existing ferry services, with no new charging beyond a berth pedestal.

phases.label: Phase 2 — full Puget Sound passenger network
phases.rationale: Extend across the full Puget Sound and the San Juan Islands network as the pilot proves out.
phases.narrative: Grow the foiling tier across the full Puget Sound and the San Juan Islands network — faster, cleaner, low-wake service the length of the system.

phases.label: Phase 3 — Regional Sound network scale
phases.rationale: Add the longer and busier domestic lines as ridership grows.
phases.narrative: A well-used domestic network on Puget Sound and the San Juan Islands as ridership grows toward the authority's published targets.

the_ask.navier_brings: The software-defined foiling fleet (Pioneer II + long-range hybrid), the Maldives-proven network playbook, certification and operations.
the_ask.partner_brings: Network integration, berth access, the published network mandate and regulatory cover.
the_ask.next_step: A Seattle commuter-channel pilot, co-specified with the authority against its published network and net-zero targets.

close.title: A zero-emission water layer that grows with the city.
close.body: Begin on the busiest commuter corridors, extend across the full Puget Sound and the San Juan Islands network, and grow into an everyday service — a zero-emission foiling tier that advances the authority's net-zero mandate while the services people rely on keep running underneath.

why_navier_now.step_change: Hydrofoiling lifts the hull clear of the water, so a Navier vessel flies instead of plowing through chop — roughly 10x more efficient than a conventional planing boat, faster (30+ kt cruise), and dramatically smoother and quieter. It's software-defined and autonomy-ready, so the same fleet keeps getting better and cheaper to run over time. A step-change in marine mobility, not an incremental faster boat.
why_navier_now.no_new_infrastructure: Navier rides on infrastructure that already exists — the open water and the piers already in use. No vertiports, no new rights-of-way, no tunnels or tracks. Pioneer II needs only a berth pedestal; the long-range hybrid needs no charging infrastructure at all. Nothing to permit, build, or wait for.
why_navier_now.the_moment: Three forces just converged: the technology crossed from prototype to platform (10 vessels delivered, 4,000+ flight hours, 2025 production sold out), decarbonization mandates turned legacy diesel fleets into stranded liabilities, and the hybrid removed the charging excuse. Autonomy is arriving on the water before the road. The marine layer is being claimed cluster-by-cluster right now.
